title: How can a ladder of divisions give the highest common factor?
description: Eighty four and one hundred eighty are divided by a shared prime, row after row, on a ladder until the last row shares no prime. The divisors on the left are multiplied to give the answer. Keeko doubts this and stops the ladder after the first row.
teaching_notes: One idea: divide both numbers by a shared prime again and again, then multiply only the divisors on the left. Watch for students who stop after the first division, or who multiply the last row as well.

source: Use the ladder for 84 and 180 to find the HCF.
video_script.why: The child can find a highest common factor from prime factorisations and now sees the ladder of divisions do the same work in rows.
video_script.substitution: Divide both numbers by a prime that goes into both, again and again, and multiply the divisors.
video_script.anchor: A ladder of division rows: the divisor on the left, the two numbers in each row, drawn as in the book.
video_script.wrong_answer: the highest common factor is two
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko stops after the first division by two. Forty two and ninety still share a prime, so the ladder must go on.
video_script.payoff_line: The highest common factor of eighty four and one hundred eighty is twelve
never_show: 2 as the highest common factor, marked right
maths_rules: 7 and 15 share no prime, so the ladder stops
video_script.design: One idea: the ladder divides until no prime is shared, and the divisors on the left multiply to the answer. The ladder grows one row per step and stays on the board.

beats.on_screen: small title card From your book; the numbers 84 and 180 side by side above an empty ladder; a question mark

marks.m1: the small title card From your book appears
marks.m2: the numbers 84 and 180 appear side by side
marks.m3: an empty ladder appears under them
marks.m4: a question mark appears beside the ladder

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Two numbers are written side by side, eighty four and one hundred eighty.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>We have to find the biggest number that divides both, by dividing in rows.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Which prime number goes into both of these numbers?

beats.on_screen: the two numbers and the empty ladder stay on the board; Keeko sits at the corner of the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: a ladder: the divisor in a column on the left, the two numbers in each row; the words prime, ladder and highest common factor appear one by one

marks.m1: the word prime appears beside the number 2
marks.m2: a divisor is written on the left and two answers in the next row
marks.m3: the rows are outlined and named ladder
marks.m4: the words highest common factor appear beside the ladder

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>We divide both numbers by a prime, which is a number whose only factors are one and itself.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The divisor is written on the left, and the two answers are written in the next row.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>These rows, one below the other, are called a ladder.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>The largest number that divides both numbers is called the highest common factor.

marks.m1: the given line is written in the working band

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Given, the two numbers are eighty four and one hundred eighty.

beats.on_screen: To find: the HCF of 84 and 180, using the ladder

marks.m1: the find line is written under the given line

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>We have to find the highest common factor, using the ladder.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: both are even, so divide by 2. Row 1: 2 | 84, 180. Row 2: 42, 90

marks.m1: the divisor 2 is written on the left of the first row
marks.m2: the new row 42, 90 is written below

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, both numbers are even, so we divide both by the prime two.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Eighty four divided by two is forty two, and one hundred eighty divided by two is ninety.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: 42 and 90 are even, so divide by 2 again. Row 3: 21, 45

marks.m1: a second divisor 2 is written on the left
marks.m2: the new row 21, 45 is written below

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, forty two and ninety are still even, so we divide by two again.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Forty two divided by two is twenty one, and ninety divided by two is forty five.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: 3 goes into 21 and 45, so divide by 3. Row 4: 7, 15. No common prime, so stop

marks.m1: the divisor 3 is written on the left
marks.m2: the last row 7, 15 is written and a stop sign appears

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, three goes into twenty one and into forty five, so we divide by three.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>That gives seven and fifteen. These two share no prime, so the ladder stops here.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: multiply the divisors on the left. HCF = 2 × 2 × 3

marks.m1: the three divisors on the left are circled
marks.m2: they are joined by multiplication signs

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, the answer is made from the divisors on the left, so we circle them.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>We multiply the divisors two, two and three.

marks.m1: the answer is written and boxed
marks.m2: the check line is written below

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>The highest common factor of eighty four and one hundred eighty is twelve.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Twelve goes into eighty four seven times, and into one hundred eighty fifteen times.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the finished ladder
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble shows only the first row with 2 | 84, 180 and the answer 2; the second row 42, 90 glows and the bubble is struck out

marks.m1: Keeko's bubble shows the first row and the answer 2
marks.m4: the full ladder returns with all three divisors lit

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko thinks the highest common factor is two, because the first division was by two.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>But forty two and ninety still share a prime, so we can divide more.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Two is only the first rung of the ladder, not the whole answer.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>We go on until the last row shares no prime. Then we multiply every divisor.
